source_text: Exstinguatur itaque indisciplinatarum expositionum libido; nihil agere contra manifestam Dei iustitiam verba credantur; quae si eius personae sunt, quam venerari necesse est, defendantur explanationibus divinae congruentibus aequitati; sin autem non metuendo sunt auctore prolata, etiam ineliquata pellantur. Igitur nunc Dei iudicio disputatur, de quo scribitur : Deus fidelis, in quo non est iniquitas; iustus et sanctus Dominus Deus [n23] . Et iterum: Iustus Dominus, et iustitiam dilexit, aequitatem vidit vultus eius [n24] . Et iterum: Omnia iudicia tua aequitas [n25] . Innumera sunt testimonia, quibus aequitas divina in sacris Voluminibus praedicatur; de qua nemo tamen vel Gentilium, vel haereticorum, praeter Manichaeos Traducianosque dubitavit.
pass_a_gloss: Let therefore the lust of undisciplined expositions be extinguished; let words be believed to do nothing against the manifest justice of God; which, if they are of that person whom it is necessary to venerate, let them be defended by explanations congruent to divine equity; but if they have been brought forth by an author not to be feared, let them be driven out even unresolved. Therefore now it is disputed about the judgment of God, of whom it is written: God is faithful, in whom there is not iniquity; just and holy is the Lord God. And again: The Lord is just, and he has loved justice, his face has seen equity. And again: All your judgments are equity. Countless are the testimonies by which divine equity is preached in the sacred Volumes; about which nevertheless no one either of the nations or of the heretics has doubted, except the Manichaeans and the Traduciani.

pass_b_english: Put an end, then, to the appetite for undisciplined interpretations. Let no words be thought capable of prevailing against God's manifest justice. If they come from someone whom we are bound to revere, defend them with explanations consistent with divine fairness. If they were spoken by an author who commands no such reverence, reject them even without resolving their meaning. We are now discussing God's judgment. Of him it is written: 'God is faithful, and in him there is no injustice; the Lord God is just and holy' (Deuteronomy 32:4) (Psalm 11:7;). And again: 'The Lord is just, and he has loved justice; his face has looked upon fairness' (Psalm 11:7; LXX Psalm 10:8) (Psalm 119:172;). And again: 'All your judgments are fairness' (Psalm 119:172; LXX Psalm 118:172). Countless testimonies in the sacred books proclaim divine fairness. Yet no one among either the nations or the heretics has doubted it, except the Manichaeans and the advocates of inherited sin.

choices.why: Julian's label for teachers of tradux peccati. Keep the polemic name as a description of transmitted sin, not as a theory of the soul's origin.
Julian's polemic target is inherited sin as a natural evil (malum naturale), the vine-layer metaphor, not a later systematic 'original sin' slogan and not soul-traducianism as such.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)
traducianism of the soul (not the load here)
